title: Chinese Robots Could Decide the AI Race
key_facts: Essay by Scott Singer (Fellow and Co-Director of the China AI Initiative) and Pavlo Zvenyhorodskyi (Senior Research Analyst), both of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Argument: China is betting on 'embodied AI', robots with AI cognition and physical autonomy, while Washington and Silicon Valley focus on large language models; if China's bet is right, the US lead in frontier models matters far less.

The authors cite the Chinese humanoid Tiangong Ultra running 100 meters in 9.39 seconds in August (and slamming into a safety wall), and Unitree's August IPO on the Shanghai Stock Exchange raising nearly $1 billion with shares up more than 450 percent on day one.
China made embodied AI a priority of its 15th Five-Year Plan; Chinese companies produce about 80 percent of the world's LiDAR sensors.
Beijing's local-government subsidy model worked for electric vehicles and solar but a five-year property slump leaves little money, and regulators are making robotics listings harder.
The authors say the US relies increasingly on Chinese robot hardware; in July the FCC banned imports of advanced foreign robots, with exemptions for US product development.

They recommend US manufacturing and talent programs, selective imports of key Chinese components, cooperation with Japan and Germany (possibly modeled on Pax Silica), and a data-sharing framework with Ukraine.
quote_evidence: China’s robotics achievements have become central to its evolving national AI strategy.

If AI-powered robots become as foundational to the global economy as Beijing hopes, countries would be as dependent on Chinese robotics supply chains as they are today for critical minerals, which has given Beijing enormous leverage over the global economy.
The longer that Washington neglects its own robotics sector, the further behind it will fall.
why_it_matters_hint: Two policy researchers argue that physical AI, not chatbots, could decide the US-China AI contest; it is an argument, not a new event.
event_date: Essay published 12 Oct 2026 (per pool); it cites events from July and August 2026
